claims.text: The stability and persistence of protective oxide layers in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C are governed by high-temperature surface segregation of X.
Al rapidly segregates to the alloy surface under oxidative or corrosive high-temperature conditions.
Si rapidly segregates to the alloy surface under oxidative or corrosive high-temperature conditions.
Surface enrichment in Al promotes the nucleation and lateral growth of a dense, coherent alumina scale.
Surface enrichment in Si promotes the nucleation and lateral growth of a dense, coherent silica scale.
Dense alumina or silica scales impede further oxidation.
Mn has a more limited surface-segregation tendency than Al or Si in these alloys.
Mn has a lower thermodynamic driving force than Al or Si for forming a stable protective oxide.
Limited Mn segregation and oxide-forming driving force lead to porous, cracked, or spalled oxide scales.
Al- and Si-containing alloys will retain more stable and coherent protective oxide layers than the Mn-containing alloy under identical exposure conditions.
The Mn-containing alloy provides a baseline characterized by unstable oxide-layer formation.
The proposed mechanism applies above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
Single-phase versus multiphase state may alter the behavior through differences in elemental diffusion kinetics.
Multielement diffusion and interactions between phases may cause deviations from the predicted oxidation behavior.

Observing an Mn-containing alloy with an oxide layer as coherent, dense, and resistant to cracking or spallation as those on the Al- or Si-containing alloys under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
